paragraphs.source_en: In my opinion, he will not keep up his evening drinking either. My master's mind, like the eyes of us cats, is always changing without pause. Whatever he undertakes, he is a man who never sticks with it for long. Besides, though in his diary he plainly shows extreme anxiety about his stomach trouble, outwardly he puts on a brave front, which is truly laughable. The other day a scholar friend of his came calling and, from a different point of view, advanced the argument: “All illness is nothing other than the result of ancestral sins and one's own sins.” His friend seemed to have studied the matter deeply; the reasoning was clear, orderly, and quite impressive. Poor master lacks both the learning and the brains to refute such a theory. But since he was just then suffering from his stomach complaint, he made every possible excuse in order to save face. He said, “Your theory is certainly novel, but you should know that Carlyle also suffered from stomach trouble.” It was an answer that had nothing to do with the point, as though he meant, “Since even Carlyle was a stomach patient, it is an honor for me to have stomach trouble too.” Thereupon his friend retorted, “Even if Carlyle had stomach trouble, not every stomach sufferer can become Carlyle.” With that one sentence, master was left speechless. Though master is so vain, in reality he still wants his stomach trouble cured, so it is rather comic that he should write in his diary, “From now on I must have two or three cups every night.” Come to think of it, the reason he dared eat so many rice cakes this morning may well have been last night's hearty drinking of Masamune with Kangetsu. Having said this, even I have begun to crave rice cakes.

paragraphs.source_en: Although I am a cat, I eat most things. I have neither the strength of old Black at the rickshaw man's house, who can make expeditions as far as the fish shop at the lane's mouth, nor, of course, the luxury-loving tastes of Miss Tortoiseshell at the two-stringed-koto teacher's house in Shinmichi, so I am not very particular about food. I eat the bread crumbs the children drop, and I also lick up fallen sweet-bean filling. As for pickles, though they are not very tasty, I have even eaten a couple of slices of pickled radish for the sake of experience. Strangely enough, once one tries eating things, almost everything turns out to be edible. To say, “I won't eat this, I won't eat that,” is a willfulness born of luxury, and in the end is not something a cat living in a teacher's house can allow himself to say. According to master, there was a novelist in France named Balzac who was an exceedingly fastidious man. However, he was not fastidious about food; being a novelist, he was fastidious to the utmost about prose. One day Balzac wanted to give a character in his novel a name; he tried all sorts of names, but none satisfied him. Just then a friend came to visit, and the two of them went out for a walk together. Naturally his friend knew nothing of the situation and merely accompanied him on the walk, but Balzac meant to use the opportunity to discover the name he had sought so hard and failed to find. So when he got out into the street, he paid attention to nothing else and walked along looking only at the shop signs. Even so, he still did not find a name that pleased him. He dragged his friend along and kept walking, while the friend, bewildered, followed him all the way. In this way they roamed all over Paris from morning until night. On the way back, Balzac happened to notice the signboard of a tailor's shop, on which was written “Marcus.” Balzac clapped his hands with delight and cried, “I've got it! I've got it! This is the only one! Marcus, what a fine name. Put a capital ‘Z’ before Marcus, and it becomes the most fitting name imaginable. Yes, it must be ‘Z’; ‘Z. Marcus’ is absolutely splendid. If one makes up a name oneself, even when one thinks it has come out well, it cannot help seeming artificial and is not very interesting. At last I have found a name that satisfies me.” He completely forgot the fatigue and confusion he had inflicted on his friend and simply rejoiced by himself. To my mind, having to spend an entire day tramping all over Paris just to name a character in a novel is far too much trouble. It is all very well to be fastidious to that degree, but one such as I, whose master is oyster-like, has no wish to be so particular. My principle is that anything is good so long as it can be eaten; perhaps my circumstances have made me so. So my present desire to eat rice cake certainly does not arise from epicurean refinement; I merely want to eat whatever I can while I can get it into my mouth. Then it occurred to me that the piece of rice cake my master had left over might still be in the kitchen. I went around to the kitchen to have a look.

paragraphs.source_zh: 我虽然是只猫儿，可一般的东西都吃。我既不像车夫家老黑那样，具有远征到胡同口鱼铺子去的力量，自然也不具备新路里教二弦琴女师傅家三毛姑娘那样喜欢奢侈，因此很少挑拣食物。我既吃孩子们吃掉下来的面包渣，也吃掉落下来的点心馅。至于咸菜嘛，虽不大可口，为了取得经验，也曾经吃过两小片咸萝卜。怪得很，不吃则已，一吃起来，差不多所有东西都能吃。这个不吃，那个不吃，这是一种来自奢侈的任性，终究不是像我这样住在教师家里的猫所能说得出口的。据主人讲，法国有个叫做巴尔扎克的小说家，是个十分考究的人。不过，他不是在饮食上考究，他是个小说家，因此在文章上极尽考究之能事。巴尔扎克有一天想给自己小说中的人物取个名字，他想了各式各样的姓名，结果都不满意。正在这时，一个朋友来玩，两人一起出去散步。当然他的朋友并不知道内情，只是陪他去散步而已，但巴尔扎克却想利用这个机会发现一个他反复求索而不可得的名字。所以他到了街上，别的什么也不顾，一路上只顾看那些店铺的招牌。不过，还是没有找到满意的名字。他带着朋友一个劲地走，他的朋友则糊里糊涂地一路紧跟。就这样，他们从早到晚转遍了整个巴黎。在回来的路上，巴尔扎克偶然看到了一家裁缝店的招牌，上面写着“马卡斯”。巴尔扎克高兴得拍着手说：“有啦！有啦！只能用它！马卡斯，多么好的名字呀。在马卡斯的前面再加上个‘Z’的大写字母，这就成了再恰当不过的名字。不错，非用‘Z’不可，‘Z. Marcus’真是妙极啦。自己编造个名字，即使觉得名字取得很好，也不免有矫揉造作之嫌，没有多大意思。这一下子可找到满意的名字啦。”他把给朋友带来的疲劳困惑忘得一干二净，自己一味地高兴。为给小说中的人物取个名字，非得花上一整天转遍全巴黎，在我看来，这未免太麻烦了。考究到如此地步，当然也不坏，不过像我这等以牡蛎般的人为主人的人，是不想去那样考究的。我主张不管什么只要能吃就好，这恐怕是境遇使然吧。所以我现在想吃年糕，决不是出于讲究吃，我只是想不管是什么，能吃到口就赶快吃。于是我就想起主人吃剩下的那块年糕可能还放在厨房里。我转到厨房去看看。
